Geological research · October 27, 2026
Ghost RiversSwift River case studyResearch mapField guide

By Paul Shoemaker · October 27, 2026

Swift River research map

Compare the modern hydrographic reference with published glacial landforms. This rectangle includes neighboring drainage areas; it is not a Swift River watershed boundary.

Loading verified source layers…

Read the evidence

Select a line or polygon to see its original source, period, confidence and limitations. The dropdown also provides keyboard access to the meltwater features.

What you are seeing

  • Solid blue: USGS NHD hydrographic segments. Their FDATE is a database date, not a current bank survey.
  • Dashed purple: published MGS meltwater-channel interpretations. The original directional arrows are not reproduced.
  • Geology polygons: published surficial unit interpretations. Qst is distinguished for comparison; its fill is not a gold-potential rating.

No hypothetical ancient Swift River course, digging target, ownership boundary, or gold-grade ranking has been added. The 72 meltwater line features are not necessarily 72 separate rivers or parts of the Swift drainage.

Sources and dates

  • Lindsay J. Spigel, Ellis Pond, map 21-8 (2021) and Roxbury, map 20-3 (2020), both 1:24,000. Original digital service. Display geometries are simplified, not survey boundaries.
  • USGS NHD flowline service, queried October 27, 2026.
  • USGS 3DEP hillshade service. Local saved export, October 27, 2026.
  • Maine GeoLibrary and statewide one-meter DEM service: a route to higher-resolution follow-up; not a separately implemented LiDAR layer here.

Still needed

Georeferenced historical photographs and map editions, independently checked channel changes, local terrace profiles and ages, and permission-specific field evidence. The MGS aerial-photo archive and USGS topoView are linked research tools, not completed historical overlays.
